newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai bank earnings seen hit by sour loans.
newsitem.headline: Thai bank earnings seen hit by sour loans.

text.p: Most of Thailand's once high-flying banks are seen posting double-digit falls in earnings this year as they are forced to make provisions to cover sour loans to the ailing property sector, analysts said.

This rare phenomenon comes into play as Thailand goes through its worst economic downturn in over a decade, with the troubled finance and cash-strapped property sectors particularly hard hit, the analysts told Reuters.
High interest rates and tight liquidity conditions were expected to raise the level of non-performing loans from the billions of dollars the banks are already saddled with, they said.
"Bank non-performing loan problems are quite serious because the economy has worsened more than earlier expected," said Kasem Prunratanamala, banking analyst at HSBC James Capel.
"We expect most of the country's 10 major banks to post negative earnings growth of about 10 to 11 percent this year," said Andrew Maule, an analyst at Vickers Ballas.
Apart from rising non-performing loans, tight liquidity, weaker non-interest rate income and narrowing profit margins were other factors seen adversely affecting bank earnings, he said.

U.S. investment bank Salomon Brothers said in a latest report that the net profits of the top eight banks were expected to fall 22 percent in 1997, hit by expected hikes in their provisions against possible loan loss.

"We have forecast a massive 216 percent increase in loan loss provisions for the eight banks covered in this report based on the expectation that non-performing loans will continue rising through 1997 into the second half of 1998," Salomon Brothers said.

Non-performing loans of eight large banks are expected to run at a level of 8.13 percent of their total loans at the end of 1997, compared with an estimate of 6.29 percent at the end of 1996, the report said.
"The increase in non-performing loans (of banks) is quite worrisome. Banks might have to raise their capital to cover their write-off of bad loans," Kasem said.
Maule said that Krung Thai Bank and Thai Military Bank would be among top large banks facing most pressure to raise capital due to their large non-performing loan exposure.
The Bank of Thailand has asked all finance companies and commercial banks to detail their non-performing loans in their second quarter financial statements due in late July.
The requirement has heightened worries in Thailand's battered stock market about the quality of bank and finance firm issues, which have been sold off quite heavily in recent weeks.

Such sales have played a key part in dragging the bourse down to eight-year lows, brokers said. Stocks in financial institutions are selling at relatively cheap prices and the sentiment is mixed as to whether now is the time to buy them or not, they added.
But some anticipated more selling of bank counters as concerns about their non-performing loans, exacerbated by Thailand's current economic woes, weighed on sentiment.
